The evaluation is broad: 17 real-world datasets, 10 random splits, controlled simulations, three modeling variants, several interval metrics, and detailed appendix tables.

Reusing the same point predictor and raw uncertainty components across several comparisons helps isolate some effects of the proposed calibration scheme. Relevant fixed-parameter and UACQR comparisons are also reported in the appendix.
The manuscript is generally clear and unusually transparent about the recommended implementation lacking an exact finite-sample conformal guarantee.
weaknesses: The evaluated and recommended algorithm selects lambda and calibrates gamma1 using the same validation outcomes, with additional model selection on that set in variants (a) and (c). Consequently, it does not possess the advertised finite-sample conformal guarantee. The separate-validation/calibration repair is not evaluated, so its accuracy and data-efficiency tradeoff remain unknown.

Algorithm 2 and the conformalized construction contain a substantive calibration error. The stated endpoint-based score equals the required multiplicative scale minus one, yet its quantile is used directly as gamma1. Either one must be added to that quantile or the score must be defined relative to the center. Thus Lemma G.2 does not establish coverage for the algorithm as written.

The most relevant ablations undermine the central two-parameter contribution: fixed gamma1=1 or fixed lambda=1 frequently match or outperform full CLEAR on held-out tests. The reported NCIW gain over the strongest component baseline, ALEATORIC-R, is only about 3%, while these ablations are omitted from the main comparison figure.

The claimed aleatoric/epistemic decomposition is not validated. In-sample residuals contain model bias and estimation error, bootstrap dispersion is not uniquely epistemic uncertainty, and the two components can overlap. No synthetic experiment measures recovery of the known components, making interpretations of lambda and the housing case study unsupported and scale-dependent.

Lemma 2.1 needs materially stronger assumptions. Centering residual-quantile widths at f yields the true conditional quantiles only when f is the conditional median, which does not cover the mean-based variant (c). Pointwise consistency at a fixed x is also insufficient by itself to conclude convergence of the global calibration quantile.

Despite conditional-coverage and extrapolation claims, real-data experiments use only random IID splits and report marginal coverage. There are no subgroup, covariate-shift, or real OOD evaluations. The synthetic study is narrow, and its multivariate plot pools dimensions whose typical radii differ substantially.

NCIW uses test outcomes to select a post-hoc calibration factor, making it an oracle diagnostic rather than deployable performance. Baseline coverage is also limited relative to the broad conformal literature, and there is no statistical comparison across datasets or meaningful runtime analysis for the extensive bootstrapping.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: constructing adaptive regression intervals that combine data-noise and model-instability signals.
CLEAR is simple, modular, and compatible with different underlying uncertainty estimators; selecting the mixture using a proper scoring rule is intuitive.
The empirical study is relatively broad, covering synthetic extrapolation settings, 17 real-world datasets, 10 splits, three model configurations, and an applied case study.
The appendix reports extensive per-dataset results, hyperparameters, multiple metrics, and useful component ablations.
Residual-based quantile modeling is a potentially useful practical idea, and empirical test coverage is generally close to nominal.
weaknesses: The central evidence for learning two calibration parameters is unconvincing. Tables 7–10 show that fixed λ=1 or fixed γ1=1 frequently matches or outperforms CLEAR, generally within the reported standard deviations. These crucial ablations are omitted from the main comparison, while the advertised 17.4% and 28.2% gains are against weaker individual components; the gain over ALEATORIC-R is only about 3% in NCIW.

The evaluated method reuses the same validation data for base-model selection, calibrating γ1, and choosing λ from more than 4,000 candidates. Consequently, it has no finite-sample conformal guarantee and is susceptible to selection overfitting. The separately calibrated variant that would restore validity is not evaluated, so its claimed performance is unknown.

Algorithm 2 and Lemma G.2 contain an algebraic error. If the preliminary bounds are f−A and f+B, the stated score equals the required multiplicative factor minus one, but the final interval scales A and B directly by that score. The construction therefore needs a +1 adjustment or a different score; as written, the claimed coverage theorem does not follow.

The asymptotic result assumes away the main problem: once a consistent conditional-quantile estimator is available, the epistemic term vanishes and ordinary quantile regression already gives the conclusion. The proof also needs an explicit conditional-median centering assumption and stronger justification for model selection and residual estimation. Mean-based variant (c) and the use of expectile GAMs do not generally satisfy these assumptions.

The claimed aleatoric/epistemic decomposition is not identified or validated. In-sample residual quantiles contain model bias and estimation error, while bootstrap spread is not necessarily a calibrated measure of epistemic uncertainty; adding their quantile widths has no probabilistic justification. Thus λ should not be interpreted as the relative source of uncertainty. The case-study formula also reverses the γ1 and γ2 weights in its purported epistemic-to-aleatoric ratio.

The primary NCIW metric performs an oracle recalibration using test labels. This is unsuitable as a headline deployment metric and can obscure calibration failures. Results also lack paired significance tests and can be dominated by catastrophic failures of individual baselines.

Conditional-coverage claims on real data are unsupported: the real-world experiments report marginal coverage and aggregate width/loss only, while conditional or extrapolation behavior is demonstrated on a narrow synthetic family. Comparisons to strong localized/conditional conformal approaches are missing.

Several reproducibility details are inconsistent, including omission of the 1/N normalization in the stated quantile-loss formula, contradictory model-table references, and no treatment of quantile crossing or zero calibration denominators.

strengths: CLEAR is a simple, modular way to combine two input-dependent uncertainty estimates while separating their relative weighting from global calibration.

weaknesses: The stated conformal construction is technically incorrect. In Algorithm 2 and Definition G.1, each score equals the required multiplicative scale minus one, yet the final interval is scaled by the score rather than one plus the score. The evaluated default method selects the base model, tunes λ over roughly 4,010 candidates, and calibrates γ1 using the same validation set. Lemma 2.1 is insufficiently justified. Centering residual quantiles around their residual median yields conditional response quantiles only when the point predictor is the conditional median; this fails in general and is particularly problematic for variant (c), whose models estimate conditional means. Evidence for the central two-parameter contribution is weak. The fixed-λ and fixed-γ1 ablations frequently match or outperform full CLEAR, but are omitted from the main comparison. The headline 28.2% and 17.4% gains concern weaker individual components; the closest ALEATORIC-R baseline is only 3% worse in NCIW on average. No paired significance tests are reported, and normalized averages are influenced by a few catastrophic baseline failures.

The evaluation does not adequately support the conditional-coverage motivation: real-data experiments use IID random splits and report marginal coverage and sharpness, while the synthetic study is narrow, lacks uncertainty bands, and even shows noticeable CLEAR undercoverage in parts of Figure 5. The learned decomposition is not identifiable: rescaling either raw component and inversely rescaling its coefficient leaves the final interval unchanged, so λ need not reveal the true balance of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The study evaluates only final intervals, not recovery of the two components, and the case-study formula reverses the coefficients in the stated epistemic-to-aleatoric ratio.

NCIW uses test labels for an additional test-time calibration and is therefore a diagnostic rather than deployable interval width. Presenting its relative improvements as plain “interval width” improvements overstates the practical result. Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the invalid formal specification, theoretical gaps, and insufficient support for the main novelty prevent acceptance at a top-tier venue.

The appendices provide algorithms, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, extensive numerical tables, and a standard finite-sample guarantee for a properly split variant.
Residual-based quantile modeling and combining complementary uncertainty signals appear practically useful relative to some individual-component baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluated default procedure tunes roughly 4,000 mixture weights on the same labels used for conformal calibration, with Dval equal to Dcal; some variants also select the base model on this set. This invalidates the advertised finite-sample conformal guarantee and creates serious selection-overfitting risk. The properly split variant introduced in Appendix G is not evaluated.

The central two-parameter contribution is not convincingly supported by its own ablations. Across Tables 7–15, fixed lambda=1 or fixed gamma1=1 frequently matches or outperforms CLEAR. The main plots omit these strongest controls and emphasize gains over individual components; the improvement over ALEATORIC-R is only about 3% NCIW in the primary configuration.

Novelty is limited: the method is essentially a nonnegative linear mixture of two interval-width features followed by scalar calibration and validation-based weight selection. Residual quantile regression is also a familiar two-stage construction. Comparisons against closely related adaptive or localized conformal methods are insufficient.

The claimed epistemic–aleatoric interpretation is not established. Bootstrap prediction dispersion measures estimator instability but can miss shared model bias, while residual quantiles can contain model error as well as irreducible noise. Their arbitrary relative scaling also makes lambda intrinsically non-identifiable, so the case-study interpretation of lambda as a scientific decomposition is unsupported.

The asymptotic conditional-coverage argument omits important conditions. Pointwise consistency does not by itself establish convergence of the calibration quantile, and the proof implicitly needs the point predictor to estimate the conditional median. This conflicts with variant (c), whose models target conditional means under potentially asymmetric noise. The finite-sample theorem applies only to the modified, unevaluated procedure and otherwise follows standard split conformal reasoning.

Real-data experiments assess almost exclusively marginal test coverage despite conditional coverage being a central motivation. The synthetic evaluation covers a narrow family of data-generating processes, and there are no paired significance analyses or convincing evaluations under subgroup or realistic distribution shift.

NCIW is computed by oracle recalibration using test labels. This can conceal severe scale failures and is unsuitable as primary evidence for deployable interval quality. Reported mean percentage gains are additionally sensitive to a few catastrophic baseline outliers.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript references supplementary code without providing a location, omits package versions and computational details, and leaves important choices such as whether residuals are in-sample or out-of-fold unclear.

weaknesses: The central methodological novelty is limited. CLEAR is essentially a validation-tuned nonnegative linear combination of two interval-width estimates followed by global scaling. A central empirical claim is contradicted by the presented plots. The stated conformalized algorithm contains an off-by-one error. With half-width w, its score is S=max((f-w-Y)/w,(Y-f-w)/w)=T-1, but it uses the quantile of S directly as the final multiplicative width. The required multiplier is S+1, or the score numerator must instead be centered at f. Consequently, Lemma B.2 does not apply to the interval as written.

The asymptotic conditional-coverage result largely assumes the hard part: consistency of the residual quantile estimator. The epistemic term then vanishes, so the result reduces to ordinary quantile-regression consistency and does not justify CLEAR's finite-sample combination. The DE/SQR experiment compares CLEAR with an epistemic-only ensemble and an aleatoric-only quantile model, so improvement from combining them is expected. Comparisons to a standard total-predictive DE, stronger adaptive conformal methods, and consistently configured UACQR are missing.

The learned weights do not identify physical aleatoric versus epistemic contributions: they also absorb arbitrary estimator scaling, misspecification, and optimization error. Thus the interpretation of lambda and the case-study claims about uncertainty-source dominance are stronger than warranted.
